first_impression.reaction: Googled 'travel advisor benefits' on the train because we're weighing up doing the Bali wedding ourselves. The intro gets to the point by the third sentence and the takeaways are short, so I kept going. Then the title confused me: it says benefits 'you cannot get booking alone' and the intro says none of it is out of reach on your own. I skimmed the six ways, read the 'what you can book yourself' questions properly and the FAQ. Bookmarked for the questions-to-ask list.

journey.quote: A good advisor is one person keeping all of it in step, with quotes in Australian dollars and every inclusion confirmed in writing before you pay.
journey.reaction: That's the answer, inside the first 100 words. Good.

journey.quote: None of that is out of reach on your own. It is simply slower, and it lands on you at the busiest point of the year.
journey.reaction: Honest, I like it. But the title literally says 'You Cannot Get Booking Alone'. So which is it?

journey.quote: Plenty of couples book their own flights and stays, and the harder parts are guests, many suppliers and payments in several currencies.
journey.reaction: Useful point but it reads oddly. I had to read it twice; feels like it wants a 'but' in the middle.

journey.section: Six ways an advisor makes a wedding trip easier
journey.quote: If the ceremony moves by a day, one conversation should flow through to flights, room nights and supplier bookings, rather than six separate emails from you.
journey.reaction: Concrete. That's exactly the mess I'm scared of.

journey.section: Six ways an advisor makes a wedding trip easier
journey.quote: Booking through an advisor does not give you stronger rights, and it does not take any away.
journey.reaction: This is number six of 'ways an advisor makes it easier', and it says the advisor changes nothing. Then it's a paragraph of legal terms. On my phone that's where I started thumbing past.

journey.section: What you can book yourself, and where it gets harder
journey.quote: If the trip is just the two of you, a handful of bookings and one currency, you may not need an advisor at all.
journey.reaction: A site that sells advisors telling me I might not need one. That makes me trust the rest more.

journey.section: What you can book yourself, and where it gets harder
journey.quote: **Who is tracking your guests?** Arrival dates, room allocations, dietary notes and the cousin who changes flights twice.
journey.reaction: Ha. That's my cousin. Bold questions are easy to scan.

journey.section: Questions to ask before you hire an advisor
journey.quote: **Do you hold insolvency insurance?** Travel provider or agent insolvency is commonly excluded from cancellation cover, and only a few insurers cover it.
journey.reaction: Never would have thought to ask this. This list is the bit I'm saving.

journey.section: Questions to ask before you hire an advisor
journey.quote: **Do you belong to an industry accreditation scheme, and what does it require?**
journey.reaction: Every other question has a line explaining why it matters. This one just sits there. What am I meant to listen for?

journey.section: Questions to ask before you hire an advisor
journey.quote: Read the Product Disclosure Statement before you buy, choose a policy that covers every country on the route including stopovers, and declare all pre-existing conditions upfront.
journey.reaction: Good advice, but after an eight-point list I get another dense insurance paragraph and a transfers paragraph. Felt like a second article.

journey.quote: Yes. Many couples book their own flights or honeymoon stays and hand over the wedding pieces.
journey.reaction: Straight answer to the thing I actually wondered. Good FAQ.

journey.quote: The fee is agreed in writing before any work begins, and the advisor confirms inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Fine, but I still don't know roughly what it costs.

unanswered_questions: Roughly what does an advisor cost, and is it a flat fee or a percentage?
Does Wedded Concierge work with couples who live outside Australia, for example in Singapore?
If I've already booked my flights, can I still use an advisor just for the wedding side with Wedded Wonderland?

turn_offs_found.quote: Travel Advisor Benefits You Cannot Get Booking Alone
turn_offs_found.why: The headline promises things you can't get on your own, then the intro says 'None of that is out of reach on your own' and the six ways section says 'None of these are shortcuts you are locked out of.' Headline and body contradict each other, which makes the headline feel like clickbait.

turn_offs_found.quote: ### Your consumer rights, booked either way
turn_offs_found.why: Listed as one of six ways an advisor makes things easier, but the section says an advisor changes nothing about your rights. Heading doesn't match the list it sits in, and it's the densest legal bit on the page.

turn_offs_found.quote: On insurance, the [Smartraveller travel insurance guide](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/travel-essentials/travel-insurance) is plain: the right policy is as essential as a passport, and the Australian Government cannot pay your bills overseas.
turn_offs_found.why: Starts a long insurance and transfers tail after the questions list. On a phone it's a wall I scrolled past; the key points could sit inside questions 5 and 8.

would_share_with: My fiance, for the 'questions to ask before you hire an advisor' list
My sister, who is trying to organise a family trip to Japan, for the 'what you can book yourself' checklist

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like to talk through your wedding and honeymoon, [speak with Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=travel-advisor-benefits&utm_content=closing).
cta_reaction.why: I came to work out whether advisors are worth it, not to hire one today. The page was fair with me and the plugs stayed short, so if Bali gets complicated I'd come back. Without any idea of cost, I'm not clicking yet.

top_3_changes: Make the title match the body: drop 'You Cannot Get Booking Alone' (the page itself says none of it is out of reach) for something like 'what an advisor makes easier'.
Move 'Your consumer rights, booked either way' out of the six ways list (or reframe it as the advisor walking you through both sets of terms) and trim the legal detail so it reads on a phone.
Fold the insurance and transfer paragraphs after the questions list into questions 5 and 8, give question 7 a one-line 'why it matters', and change the third takeaway's 'and' to 'but'.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Priya, a casual Google searcher on a phone
No invented brand facts; missing info went to unanswered_questions
Journey types limited to gained_trust, lost_trust, confused, bored, excited, objection
Deferred business details (fee basis, commissions, who is on the ground, scale proof, perks, Wedded Privileges) not treated as must-fix; cost question kept in unanswered_questions only

assumptions: Persona is provisional (weight 0.10); reactions reflect generic informational search intent.

Arrived from a Google search for 'travel advisor benefits' on a phone with a 3-minute budget; read intro, takeaways, 'what you can book yourself', the questions list and FAQ, skimmed the six ways and the insurance tail.
Framed as an Australian living in Singapore, weighing a DIY Bali wedding against using an advisor (consistent with earlier Priya readings).
Advisor cost is a deferred business detail, so it is raised as an unanswered question and in the CTA reaction, not as a must-fix change.
Image slots and HTML comments treated as invisible.
